topic: Plaintext MLLP Feeds Cripple FHIR Zero-Trust
postText:
Most hospital integration engines hold a dangerous secret. Behind shiny, encrypted FHIR APIs lies raw HL7 v2 over naked MLLP.

In healthcare IT, modernization often means putting an API gateway in front of 30-year-old bedside telemetry protocols. HL7 v2 relies on Minimal Lower Layer Protocol (MLLP)—unencrypted plain TCP without native authentication.

When bridging legacy telemetry into FHIR datastores, engineers often make a fatal mistake: terminating MLLP inside an open network and mapping it straight to FHIR Observation resources using a single privileged service account. This silently strips patient audit provenance. If a compromised infusion pump or rogue node injects falsified vitals, the FHIR server signs off on it blindly.

To lock this down:
1. Isolate legacy MLLP adapters in dedicated zero-trust ingress enclaves with mutual TLS wrappers.
2. Synthesize FHIR Provenance records at the boundary, binding verified source MAC and network signatures.
3. Replace broad service tokens with ephemeral SMART-on-FHIR scopes derived from verified device context.

Healthcare integration is never just format conversion; it is threat modeling legacy protocol debt against modern trust boundaries.

How does your team enforce zero-trust identity when ingesting legacy biomedical device streams?
